summary: This project entails a graphical historical review of fire hotspots using data from VIIRS and MODIS. Accessible via an interactive website, it allows users to customize their view by state, date range, model, harmonization and forecast. Furthermore, users can export the results as a calendar image, a map, or a CSV file containing daily, monthly or regional data.
details:
Every spring Mexico burns, and since 2012 the satellites that count that fire have changed. NASA's older MODIS sensor sees 1 km pixels; the newer VIIRS sees 375 m and reports about 3.9 times more hotspots in Mexico. Put the two records side by side and burning appears to quadruple overnight, though only the instrument changed. Our project, Burn Calendar, fixes that and makes the result usable.

How it works

We apply filtering to both sensors and weight each VIIRS detection by historical MODIS and VIIRS ratio for the specific state and month-pulling noisy, low-data cells toward the national baseline. The result is a seamless 25-year series (2020 - 2025) measured in one consistent unit: the MODIS equivalent hotspot.<

  • Proven Accuracy: On unseen test years (2020–2025), our series matches MODIS within 2.1% nationally.
  • Granular Precision: Calibrating by state and month cuts regional error by 33% to 50% compared to a single national conversion factor.

Interactive Exploration & Forecasting Our browser-based web app turns raw satellite detections into an accessible analytical tool:

  • Custom Views: Filter by all of Mexico, individual states, or custom map rectangles across any date range.
  • Visual Analytics: Explore a color-ramp burn calendar, historical anomaly views, and a 3-layer spatial density map.
  • Actionable Forecasts: Generate 30-day, 12-week, and 12-month outlooks with 80% confidence intervals—matching national climatology while outperforming naive "same-as-last-year" baselines.
  • Instant Exports: Download publication-ready PNGs or customized historical and forecast CSVs.

Why It Matters

Roughly two-thirds (66%) of Mexico's annual hotspots occur in April and May. Giving authorities a unified historical baseline and seasonal forecast lets them deploy fire crews, launch prevention campaigns, and issue early alerts before peak season hits.

Tech Stack & Scientific Rigor

  • Built With: Python (pandas, numpy, geopandas, shapely, pyarrow), JavaScript/Node.js, NASA FIRMS data, and geoBoundaries.
  • Methodology & Transparency: We accounted for sensor resolution gaps, seasonality, and small-sample noise—discarding features that degraded out-of-sample accuracy. We also state our scope clearly: a thermal hotspot is not a burned area, 2000–2002 data is extrapolated, and the 2026 forecast awaits near-real-time verification.
